parameters.description:
What narrows a realtime watch, keyed by dataset. Requires `config.is_realtime: true`,
and goes at the top level of the body rather than inside `config`.

A record the live search just found is too new for its own index to hold, so narrowing
asks about the durable entity behind it instead: the author of a post, the company
hiring for a job, the person as the index already knows them. Each block is a plain
single-dataset tree asked of that dataset's own index, in that dataset's own
vocabulary, so a field belonging to another dataset is refused rather than resolved.

A block keeps that dataset's **full search grammar**, unlike `realtime_filters`: an
`or` across two different fields, nested `and` / `or` groups, and every negation
operator all work, because an index answers it rather than the live search. The one
restriction is that every leaf must belong to the block's own dataset. The fields and
operators are exactly those of that dataset's search endpoint: `PersonSearchCondition`
on `POST /person/search` for the `person` block, and `SearchCondition` on
`POST /company/search` for the `company` block.

Only `person` and `company` may be named, and which of the two depends on the watch:
a `person` or `social_post` watch may narrow on either, and a `company` or `job` watch
on `company` alone. Name one block. A job posting or a social post is the new record
itself, so there is no older copy of it to ask about, and a condition about the record
the search returned belongs in `realtime_filters`.

A record whose entity the index does not hold is dropped rather than delivered
unchecked. Immutable once set, like `realtime_filters`.

schema.description: Schedule and per-run caps for a discovery watch.

expires_at.description: Auto-expire date, `YYYY-MM-DD`. The watch stops running after it.

is_realtime.description:
Run each search against a live search rather than the Crustdata index, so the watch
finds records as they appear on the web. Requires `realtime_filters`, and puts the
watch on the 1-day SLA.

Four things change when this is `true`. `filters` is refused, and
`narrowing_filters` is what narrows the watch instead. `trigger.every_hours` must be
`24` or more, because a live run retrieves from the web and is billed per new
record.
On `person` and `company`, `realtime_filters` may not match more than 10,000
records, counted on that tree alone: those live searches report a total, so a
broad watch is refused at creation. The `job` and `social_post` searches page
through results instead of counting them, so no total exists to check and a broad
watch is accepted.
And delivery costs 150 credits per new record on every dataset, the 1-day SLA rate,
rather than the 0.5 or 2 a 30-day SLA watch pays.

Immutable, like `realtime_filters` and `narrowing_filters`: all three define the
watch rather than schedule it, so a `PATCH` carrying any of them is refused and you
create a new watch instead. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes it back,
alongside a `refresh_frequency_days` reporting the SLA the watch bills at: `1` when
realtime, `30` otherwise.

This flag is the only thing that picks how a discovery watch reads. Sending
`config.refresh_frequency_days` on a discovery watch is refused whatever its value.

max_results_per_run.description:
Most records to deliver in one run. The first, baseline run is always capped at 5
regardless of this value.

A value above 1000 requires `config.payload_delivery_type` of `link`. Inline delivery
posts its chunks one after another, so it stops at 1000 records per run, while a link
run is always one request. The rule reads both keys together and applies on create and
on PATCH, so a PATCH is checked against the watch as it will be: raising the cap on a
link watch is accepted, raising it alone on an inline watch is not, and switching a
watch that already carries a cap above 1000 back to inline is refused.

payload_delivery_type.description:
Where the run's records travel. `inline` puts them in the notification body under
`results`, split across several requests when a run is large. `link` leaves the body
carrying no records at all and adds `metadata.payload_delivery`, a pre-signed S3 URL
for one NDJSON file holding every record of the run.

`link` is required when `config.max_results_per_run` is above 1000, because inline
delivery stops at 1000 records per run.

Switch to `link` when a run can exceed what your receiver accepts: an AWS Lambda proxy
integration caps a request at 6 MB and an ALB target at 1 MB, and an oversize body is
refused whole. `inline` is never overridden by size, so a large run stays inline and
is split instead.

Mutable. Changing it leaves the watch's filters, tracked fields, and sort order
untouched, but a `config` PATCH is validated whole, so send the current `trigger`
alongside it. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes the stored value under
`config.payload_delivery_type`, but that is the watch's setting rather than what a
given run did: read `metadata.payload_delivery.type` on a notification, or
`payload_delivery.type` on a run summary, to see which mode a run actually used, since
a `link` watch falls back to `inline` when the file cannot be written.

preferred_hour.description: Hour of day, in UTC, to prefer for the run.

trigger.description: How often the watch runs. Interval is the only trigger type today.

every_hours.description: Hours between runs, for example `1`, `6`, `24`, or `168`.

type.description: Trigger type.

is_realtime.description:
Run each search against a live search rather than the Crustdata index, so the watch
finds records as they appear on the web. Requires `realtime_filters`, and puts the
watch on the 1-day SLA.

Four things change when this is `true`. `filters` is refused, and
`narrowing_filters` is what narrows the watch instead. `trigger.every_hours` must be
`24` or more, because a live run retrieves from the web and is billed per new
record.
On `person` and `company`, `realtime_filters` may not match more than 10,000
records, counted on that tree alone: those live searches report a total, so a
broad watch is refused at creation. The `job` and `social_post` searches page
through results instead of counting them, so no total exists to check and a broad
watch is accepted.
And delivery costs 150 credits per new record on every dataset, the 1-day SLA rate,
rather than the 0.5 or 2 a 30-day SLA watch pays.

Immutable, like `realtime_filters` and `narrowing_filters`: all three define the
watch rather than schedule it, so a `PATCH` carrying any of them is refused and you
create a new watch instead. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes it back,
alongside a `refresh_frequency_days` reporting the SLA the watch bills at: `1` when
realtime, `30` otherwise.

This flag is the only thing that picks how a discovery watch reads. Sending
`config.refresh_frequency_days` on a discovery watch is refused whatever its value.

max_results_per_run.description:
Most records to deliver in one run. The first, baseline run is always capped at 5
regardless of this value.

A value above 1000 requires `config.payload_delivery_type` of `link`. Inline delivery
posts its chunks one after another, so it stops at 1000 records per run, while a link
run is always one request. The rule reads both keys together and applies on create and
on PATCH, so a PATCH is checked against the watch as it will be: raising the cap on a
link watch is accepted, raising it alone on an inline watch is not, and switching a
watch that already carries a cap above 1000 back to inline is refused.

payload_delivery_type.description:
Where the run's records travel. `inline` puts them in the notification body under
`results`, split across several requests when a run is large. `link` leaves the body
carrying no records at all and adds `metadata.payload_delivery`, a pre-signed S3 URL
for one NDJSON file holding every record of the run.

`link` is required when `config.max_results_per_run` is above 1000, because inline
delivery stops at 1000 records per run.

Switch to `link` when a run can exceed what your receiver accepts: an AWS Lambda proxy
integration caps a request at 6 MB and an ALB target at 1 MB, and an oversize body is
refused whole. `inline` is never overridden by size, so a large run stays inline and
is split instead.

Mutable. Changing it leaves the watch's filters, tracked fields, and sort order
untouched, but a `config` PATCH is validated whole, so send the current `trigger`
alongside it. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes the stored value under
`config.payload_delivery_type`, but that is the watch's setting rather than what a
given run did: read `metadata.payload_delivery.type` on a notification, or
`payload_delivery.type` on a run summary, to see which mode a run actually used, since
a `link` watch falls back to `inline` when the file cannot be written.

`geo_exclude`): it would match subjects with some *other* matching row rather than
subjects with none. List the values you do want instead.

a real change is detected.

20 at 7, 50 at 3, 150 at 1. A value between two tiers is billed at the fresher tier.

with no backing asset makes the create fail. Company watches have a higher minimum than

entities.description:
The records to watch, as a map of identifier type to values. The accepted keys are exactly the
ones the dataset's enrich endpoint accepts, and they are resolved to canonical ids when the
watch runs. One watch holds up to 10,000 subjects across all keys.

People accept `professional_network_profile_urls` and `business_emails`. Companies accept
`domains`, `names`, `professional_network_profile_urls`, and `crustdata_company_ids`. Company
ids must be positive integers; every other identifier is a non-empty string.

headers.description: Extra headers to send with each delivery, for routing or authentication on your side.

field.description:
Dot-path into the record, addressing the same structure the dataset's enrich endpoint
returns: the fields of `POST /person/enrich` or `POST /company/enrich` are the fields a
watch can track, and there is no separate list. An array path takes `added`; a field
inside an array's items, or any single value, takes `changed`, `increased`/`decreased`
or a comparison. A field that identifies an array item cannot take `changed`, since a
new value there is a new item, and arrays can be tracked at most two levels deep.

keys.description:
Which fields identify an element of the array, in place of the identity the dataset gives
it. Valid only with `added`: on any other operator the create returns `400` with
`track: 'keys' is only valid with 'added', not '<type>'`. A string entry is one field; a
nested entry is a composite of several fields. Entries are matched as a union, so an
element is already known when any one entry matches, and the loosest entry therefore
wins: give a fallback entry the same fields as the entry it backs up. An entry cannot
identify an element when any field in that entry is null. The fields must belong to the
array's own elements and your key must be entitled to each one, so `keys` on an array of
plain strings returns `400`. A watch remembers every identity it has seen on the array,
so an element that leaves and returns does not fire again. An empty list or a bare
string returns `400` with
`track: '<path>': 'keys' must be a non-empty list of fields or field groups`.

type.description:
`changed` fires when a scalar becomes different from the last snapshot. `added` fires
when a new element appears in an array. `increased` and `decreased` fire when a number
moves up or down from the last snapshot, for example `headcount.total` growing; they take
no `value` and are refused on a field that is not a number. The comparison operators fire
when the comparison flips from false to true, for example `professional_network.connections`
crossing 500.

value.description: The threshold to compare against. Required for the comparison operators, omitted for `changed`, `added`, `increased` and `decreased`.

new_records_count.description: Records this run delivered. It is below `records_after_filter` when the cap cut the run short.

notifications.description:
Every delivery this run attempted, with the records it carried. Empty unless `status` is
`SUCCESS`: a run can leave rows behind without ever paying for or delivering them, and
those rows are not readable here.

When `payload_delivery.type` is `link`, each entry keeps its outcome (`sent_at`,
`http_status`) and drops `payload`: the records are in the linked file, and repeating
the link per entry would only be noise.

items.description: One delivery attempt made by this run, with the records it carried.

payload.description:
The delivered content, in its stored form. Absent when the run's
`payload_delivery.type` is `link`.

notifications.description:
One entry per delivered record, in its stored form. Every entry carries a stable
`uid` and the record itself under `record`. An entity entry adds `changes`; a
discovery entry adds `entity_id` and `updated_at`. The `record` is the same
shape your channel receives, so a watch's results are readable here even when no
channel is configured.

payload_delivery.description:
Where the records of this delivery actually travelled. Present on every notification and on
every run summary, so read `type` before reaching for `url`.

An `inline` delivery carries `{"type": "inline"}` and nothing else, and its records sit in the
body under `results`. A `link` delivery carries the whole block and no records: fetch `url`
with a plain `GET` and no `authorization` header, since the pre-signed S3 URL carries its own
authentication in the query string.

The file is NDJSON, one complete JSON object per line with no wrapping array, so you can stream
it without holding the run in memory. Each line is the record the inline body would have
carried: the raw dataset record for a discovery watch, without the `added` wrapper, and the
same `{changes, record}` object for an entity watch.

A watch set to `link` still reports `inline` here when the file could not be written. The
delivery then carries its records in the body as usual, so an outage costs the link and not the
notification.

bytes.description: Size of the linked file. Present only when `type` is `link`.

expires_at.description:
When `url` stops working, five days after it was issued. Present only when `type` is
`link`. Reading the run again from the run-summary endpoint issues a fresh link over
the same records.

format.description: Format of the linked file. Present only when `type` is `link`.

type.description: Where the records of this delivery travelled.

url.description:
Pre-signed S3 URL for the run's file. Present only when `type` is `link`. Fetch it when
the notification arrives rather than storing it: the signature stops working at
`expires_at`.

records_after_filter.description:
New records the run found, before the cap. On a discovery watch, the new matches. On an
entity watch, the entities that changed, and on its first run every subject Crustdata
resolved.

records_matched.description:
Entity watches only. Identifiers that resolved to a record Crustdata holds. A gap between
this and `records_searched` is the part of your list that matches nothing, which a run
would otherwise pass over in silence. `null` on a discovery run.

records_searched.description:
What the run started from. On a discovery watch, everything the query returned before the
new-record check and the cap; on a realtime discovery watch, the rows the live retrieval
returned. On an entity watch, the identifiers you listed in `entities`.

records_stale.description:
Discovery watches only. Matches an earlier run already handled, so `records_searched`
minus `records_stale` is `records_after_filter`. On a job or post watch it counts the
records posted before the last run. `null` on an entity run.

is_realtime.description:
Run each search against a live search rather than the Crustdata index, so the watch
finds records as they appear on the web. Requires `realtime_filters`, and puts the
watch on the 1-day SLA.

Four things change when this is `true`. `filters` is refused, and
`narrowing_filters` is what narrows the watch instead. `trigger.every_hours` must be
`24` or more, because a live run retrieves from the web and is billed per new
record.
On `person` and `company`, `realtime_filters` may not match more than 10,000
records, counted on that tree alone: those live searches report a total, so a
broad watch is refused at creation. The `job` and `social_post` searches page
through results instead of counting them, so no total exists to check and a broad
watch is accepted.
And delivery costs 150 credits per new record on every dataset, the 1-day SLA rate,
rather than the 0.5 or 2 a 30-day SLA watch pays.

Immutable, like `realtime_filters` and `narrowing_filters`: all three define the
watch rather than schedule it, so a `PATCH` carrying any of them is refused and you
create a new watch instead. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes it back,
alongside a `refresh_frequency_days` reporting the SLA the watch bills at: `1` when
realtime, `30` otherwise.

This flag is the only thing that picks how a discovery watch reads. Sending
`config.refresh_frequency_days` on a discovery watch is refused whatever its value.

max_results_per_run.description:
Most records to deliver in one run. The first, baseline run is always capped at 5
regardless of this value.

A value above 1000 requires `config.payload_delivery_type` of `link`. Inline delivery
posts its chunks one after another, so it stops at 1000 records per run, while a link
run is always one request. The rule reads both keys together and applies on create and
on PATCH, so a PATCH is checked against the watch as it will be: raising the cap on a
link watch is accepted, raising it alone on an inline watch is not, and switching a
watch that already carries a cap above 1000 back to inline is refused.

payload_delivery_type.description:
Where the run's records travel. `inline` puts them in the notification body under
`results`, split across several requests when a run is large. `link` leaves the body
carrying no records at all and adds `metadata.payload_delivery`, a pre-signed S3 URL
for one NDJSON file holding every record of the run.

`link` is required when `config.max_results_per_run` is above 1000, because inline
delivery stops at 1000 records per run.

Switch to `link` when a run can exceed what your receiver accepts: an AWS Lambda proxy
integration caps a request at 6 MB and an ALB target at 1 MB, and an oversize body is
refused whole. `inline` is never overridden by size, so a large run stays inline and
is split instead.

untouched, but a `config` PATCH is validated whole, so send the current `trigger`
alongside it. A create, `GET`, or `PATCH` response echoes the stored value under
`config.payload_delivery_type`, but that is the watch's setting rather than what a
given run did: read `metadata.payload_delivery.type` on a notification, or
`payload_delivery.type` on a run summary, to see which mode a run actually used, since
a `link` watch falls back to `inline` when the file cannot be written.

ones the dataset's enrich endpoint accepts, and they are resolved to canonical ids when the
watch runs. One watch holds up to 10,000 subjects across all keys.

People accept `professional_network_profile_urls` and `business_emails`. Companies accept
`domains`, `names`, `professional_network_profile_urls`, and `crustdata_company_ids`. Company

field.description:

returns: the fields of `POST /person/enrich` or `POST /company/enrich` are the fields a
watch can track, and there is no separate list. An array path takes `added`; a field
inside an array's items, or any single value, takes `changed`, `increased`/`decreased`
or a comparison. A field that identifies an array item cannot take `changed`, since a
new value there is a new item, and arrays can be tracked at most two levels deep.

Which fields identify an element of the array, in place of the identity the dataset gives
it. Valid only with `added`: on any other operator the create returns `400` with
`track: 'keys' is only valid with 'added', not '<type>'`. A string entry is one field; a
nested entry is a composite of several fields. Entries are matched as a union, so an
element is already known when any one entry matches, and the loosest entry therefore
wins: give a fallback entry the same fields as the entry it backs up. An entry cannot
identify an element when any field in that entry is null. The fields must belong to the
array's own elements and your key must be entitled to each one, so `keys` on an array of
plain strings returns `400`. A watch remembers every identity it has seen on the array,
so an element that leaves and returns does not fire again. An empty list or a bare
string returns `400` with
`track: '<path>': 'keys' must be a non-empty list of fields or field groups`.

no `value` and are refused on a field that is not a number. The comparison operators fire
when the comparison flips from false to true, for example `professional_network.connections`
crossing 500.

type.description: Filter operator. Use '=' for exact match, '!=' for not equal, '<' and '>' for exclusive numeric/date comparisons, '=<' for less-than-or-equal, '=>' for greater-than-or-equal, 'in'/'not_in' for set membership (value must be an array), 'is_null'/'is_not_null' for null checks (value must be a literal null and the `value` key is required; on nested-array fields, 'is_null' matches profiles where no element carries the field and 'is_not_null' matches profiles where at least one element has a non-null value), 'has_all' for cross-element matching on a nested-array field (value must be a non-empty array; each listed value must be matched by some array element, possibly different elements ,  shorthand for an `all_of` group of one equality condition per value), '(.)' for case-insensitive all-words match (every query word must appear, in any order; a piped value is split into separate words that must ALL match (AND), not OR; on some fields it also matches close misspellings, so use '=' or 'in' for known values and '[.]' for exact words), '(!)' for case-insensitive fuzzy negation (excludes substring matches of `value`), '[.]' for case-insensitive exact-phrase match (words must be contiguous and in order), 'geo_distance' for geographic radius inclusion, and 'geo_exclude' for geographic radius exclusion ('geo_distance' keeps profiles inside the radius, 'geo_exclude' removes them; both take an object with `location` or `lat_lng`, plus `distance` and optional `unit`). Use '=<' and '=>' instead of '<=' and '>='. For cross-element logic beyond a single value list, use an `all_of` group (see PersonSearchConditionGroup). On free-text fields such as basic_profile.summary, '=', '!=', 'in' and 'not_in' match a phrase, not the whole value, and 'in' and 'not_in' take at most 1,000 values.

value.description: Filter value. Type depends on operator: For '=', '!=', '<', '>', '=<', '=>': string or number. For 'in', 'not_in': array of strings or numbers. For 'is_null', 'is_not_null': a literal null ,  the `value` key is still required. For 'has_all': non-empty array of strings or numbers (nested-array fields only). For '(.)': string. A '|' in the value is a word separator, not OR: "VP|Director" matches the same profiles as "VP Director". To match any one of several values, put one '(.)' condition for each value in an `or` group. For '(!)': string; rows whose value contains this substring (case-insensitive) are excluded. Unlike '(.)' / '[.]', multi-word values are matched as a literal phrase (not word-split): `(!) "New York"` excludes only rows that literally contain "New York", not "New Yorker"; send separate `(!)` conditions inside an `and` group to exclude on each word independently. For '[.]': string substring to match. For 'geo_distance'/'geo_exclude': object with one of {location: string} or {lat_lng: [lat, lng]}, plus {distance: number, unit: "km"|"mi"|"miles"|"m"|"ft"}.
